Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I think about why the event has happened to me
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

vignette: John, a 76-year-old widowed European man who worked as a cashier, experienced profound psychological distress after surviving a civilian war zone. The trauma had left him with persistent symptoms that significantly impacted his daily life and well-being. The traumatic event was vividly etched in John's memory. He recalled the intense sounds of explosions, the chaos, and the fear that gripped everyone around him. These memories were mostly visual images, which replayed as if they were happening right now, leaving him feeling completely numb and detached, as if he were an observer rather than a participant. John’s belief that the world was dangerous had only intensified over time, feeding into his hypervigilance and constant watchfulness. He found himself constantly scanning his surroundings for any signs of threat, even in the most mundane settings such as grocery stores or at home. This hyperalertness made it hard for him to relax, causing significant sleep disturbances. He would lay awake at night, convinced that he needed to stay alert. These negative appraisals had a profound effect on how John remembered and processed his trauma. His belief that the world was dangerous made him relive those terrifying moments more frequently and vividly. When he recalled the event, it felt as though it were happening again, intensifying his emotional numbness and making it difficult to engage with the present. John’s maladaptive strategies had developed in response to these overwhelming feelings of threat and memory intrusions. He began avoiding driving altogether due to the intense anxiety it triggered, which was compounded by memories of vehicles being targeted during the war. Pushing away positive emotions felt like a necessary self-defense mechanism because he believed that feeling good could lead to a false sense of security, only to be shattered again. Over time, John’s avoidance behaviors had consequences that affected his daily life and work as a cashier. He started to isolate himself from social interactions, pushing away even the small joys and connections that usually brought him comfort. His coworkers noticed changes in his demeanor and behavior; he became more withdrawn and less engaged with customers. This reinforced his belief that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. John’s hypervigilance also extended to his interactions with others, as he would watch them closely for signs of harm. This constant state of alertness made it nearly impossible for him to trust anyone fully, leading to a sense of disconnection from those around him. His faith in people and life itself had diminished significantly, contributing to a pervasive feeling of emptiness. The cycle of these maladaptive strategies further perpetuated his negative appraisals and heightened threat perceptions. Avoiding positive feelings and driving made it difficult for John to engage meaningfully with the world, reinforcing his belief that he was no longer capable or safe. His memories became more intrusive as he isolated himself, leading to a self-reinforcing loop of fear and avoidance. What finally brought John to seek help were the mounting consequences of his symptoms: increasing isolation from friends, withdrawal from activities he once enjoyed, and difficulties at work. He realized that he was losing parts of himself that he valued deeply. Despite his fears, John hoped for a sense of safety and connection that felt increasingly out of reach. In summary, John’s traumatic experience had reshaped his perception of the world, leading to intense hypervigilance, avoidance behaviors, and pervasive negative appraisals about his capabilities and trust in others. These interwoven factors created a self-reinforcing cycle that had significantly impacted his daily life and well-being.
